subtype: Using skills for a purpose beyond self [Actor]

"You're drawing shelves again?" Aparna asked, carrying two plates of curd rice to the table.
"Library shelves," Rukmini said, not looking up from her sketch. "For the government school near the bus depot. Low ones, so the little kids can reach."
"Don't you draw buildings all day at the firm?"
"Glass offices for people who already have everything." Rukmini finally put her pencil down. "I like my job, okay? I'm not unhappy. I just want my drawings to do something for someone."
"So you're happy and not happy."
"Exactly." Rukmini laughed. "Content and itchy."
"And when the shelves are done? Then you'll be satisfied?"
"Then the headmistress wants a reading corner. Then maybe a ramp for the side gate." She shrugged. "I don't think there's a finish line, Aparna. I think it just keeps going."
Aparna pushed a plate toward her. "Eat first. Then save the world."

qa.a: Near the bus depot.

I'm Aparna. When I think back to last year, I remember how strange I felt. I was twenty-five, a sous chef at a good hotel in Pune. I liked my kitchen and my team. I was, honestly, content. But on my days off I'd feel this itch, as if something was waiting for me.
In June, my friend Rukmini, who coordinates a women's shelter, asked if I could teach one cooking class. I went on a Monday with a bag of vegetables and a borrowed tawa. Eight women, some shy, some bossy, and by the end they were calling me Didi. By the end we were arguing happily about how much chilli goes in poha.
That one class became every Monday. Two of the women now cook for a canteen.
I thought teaching would scratch the itch and that would be that. It didn't. Now I'm learning to teach better, and planning a baking month. It feels less like finishing and more like starting.

qa.q: What did Aparna carry to her first class?
qa.a: A bag of vegetables and a borrowed tawa.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel on her days off before she began teaching?
qa.a: She felt content with her work but restless, with an itch as if something was waiting for her.

qa.a: They may enjoy the lively, arguing kitchen, and for some the classes have led to real work cooking for a canteen.

grounding: It shows a young professional who is content yet restless, uses her cooking skills to teach women at a shelter and finds that growth keeps going rather than ending.

I'm Deepak, fourth floor. Mahima cooks for three flats in our building, including ours. She's about twenty-four, sends most of her pay home to her village, and lives in a tiny room above the garages.
Last winter I noticed a sheet of cardboard on her kitchen stool. She had drawn a computer keyboard on it in pen, every key. Between stirring the dal and rolling rotis, she'd tap the letters with her fingers, whispering. When I asked, she smiled, embarrassed. "The free class at the public library is on Sundays. They have only four computers, so I practise here."
She didn't wait to afford a laptop or for a better room. She borrowed my old newspapers to copy sentences for typing speed.
In March she showed me a certificate from the library course. Now she wants to learn spreadsheets. I don't know how hard those months were for her. She never complained once.

qa.q: What did Mahima draw on the sheet of cardboard?
qa.a: A computer keyboard, every key.

qa.a: It suggests she felt a little shy about being seen practising on a drawing, but also quietly determined to learn.

Week one. Jasleen, twenty-five, sat behind the counter of her uncle's hardware shop in Ludhiana, writing a Punjabi poem on the back of an old receipt. She had no notebook, no quiet room, and no time except between customers asking for hinges. She wrote four lines anyway and folded the receipt into her pocket.
Week four. Her cousin Rajni found a stack of receipts in Jasleen's cupboard, all covered in writing. "You should read these somewhere." There was a free open-mic evening at the district library. Jasleen went in her work clothes, hands shaking, and read one poem.
Week nine. The library's little newsletter printed her poem about a nail that holds up a whole door. Jasleen still wrote on receipts. She just bought a clip to keep them together, and began a new one that same afternoon, between two customers.

I'm Kiran, Baljeet's big sister. I'm ten. Yesterday we went to buy his new school shoes. The shop uncle knelt down to tie the laces for him.
Baljeet pulled his foot back and pushed the uncle's hand away. "Me! I'm five!"
Everyone waited. He crossed the laces, made one loop, lost it, made it again. His tongue was poking out. It took forever. The bow was wobbly.
Then he stood up and stamped his feet and looked at all of us like he had won a race.

subtype: Wants to choose own subject and friends [Actor]
passage:
I'm Nirmala, and looking back at Class 11, I think that was the year I figured out I was a separate person from my parents.
It started with Tenzin. She's in my class, plays guitar in a band, wears too many bracelets. Amma thought she was a "distraction" for her daughter and wanted me to sit with Priyamvada, who tops every test. I said no. Tenzin was the first person who asked what I thought, not what I scored.
Then came the stream fight. Appa had already paid the deposit for Science coaching. I wanted Humanities, because I wanted to study why people do what they do. We shouted, I cried, Appa went silent for two days.
It wasn't that I didn't love them. It was that if I couldn't choose my own friend and my own subjects, I didn't know who I would be. In the end we agreed I'd try Humanities for one term. I'm still there.

qa.q: What did Appa pay the deposit for?
qa.a: Science coaching.

qa.q: Why did choosing her own friend and subjects matter so much to Nirmala?
qa.a: She felt that without choosing them she would not know who she was, which is why the fights left her so upset that she shouted and cried.

qa.q: What turning point ended the clash, and why was it a sensible step?
qa.a: Agreeing to try Humanities for one term gave Nirmala her choice while giving her parents a way to accept it without feeling ignored.

qa.q: How might Amma have seen Tenzin, and why might Nirmala see her differently?
qa.a: Amma saw Tenzin as a distraction, but Nirmala valued her as the first person who asked what she thought rather than what she scored.

grounding: It shows a teenager who wants to choose her own friend and stream, clashes with her parents' plans and feels independence as part of who she is.

Counsellor's note, Thursday. Indu Kapoor, school counsellor.
Vaibhav (Class 11) came in at lunch, jaw tight, and sat on the edge of the chair. His parents enrolled him in an engineering coaching batch over the weekend without asking him. They also told him to stop spending time with his friend Sunny, whom they call a bad influence because he skips tuition.
Vaibhav said, "I'm sixteen. I can't choose my subject, I can't choose my friends. Then what is mine?" He wants to take Commerce and says Sunny is the only one who listens to him. He was angry, but his voice cracked when he said he doesn't want to fight with his mother.
I listened and did not take sides. I told him his wish to decide is a normal part of growing up. Next steps: with his permission, a meeting with Vaibhav and his parents next week, so each can explain their reasons.

"Bees?" Ammi put the ladle down. "Kiran, my son, you have a B.Sc. in chemistry."
"I know, Ammi. Which is why I understand the bees better."
"Your cousin has a bank job. Pension, everything."
"And he hates it." Kiran sat on the kitchen stool. "There's a honey farm near Mahabaleshwar. They'll train me for a year. Very little money."
"And if it fails?"
"Then it fails and I learn something. But I've spent every holiday reading about bees. I've never read one page about banking by choice."
Ammi turned back to the stove. "Your Abbu won't like it."
"I know." Kiran's voice softened. "I'll call every Sunday. I'll come for Eid. I'm not running away from you, Ammi. I'm running toward something."
Ammi was quiet a long time. Then, without turning, she said, "Take the good blanket. It's cold up there."

I'm Vijay. Two years ago, at twenty, I walked out of my CA articleship and took a job as a mechanic and ride guide with a small cycling-tour company in the Himalaya. Papa called it "a hobby pretending to be a job" and said his son was throwing his life away. He didn't come to see me off at the station.
The first season was hard. I slept in tents, fixed punctures in the snow, and earned less than my friends spent on phones. There were nights I lay awake thinking, what if Papa's right?
But then there were mornings above the clouds, when a group of strangers made it up a pass I'd planned, and I'd feel so free I wanted to shout.
My sister Sarita sent me the family news every week. I sent Ma a photo every evening from wherever I was. I missed them all the time. I just couldn't live their route.
This spring, Papa asked Sarita to forward him my photos too.

qa.q: What did Papa call Vijay's new job?
qa.a: A hobby pretending to be a job.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling on the nights he lay awake?
qa.a: He felt doubt and worry that Papa might be right, even though he had chosen this path himself.

qa.a: It suggests Papa is softening and wants to share in his son's life, even if he never approved of the path.

"Revathi, sit. Your Kamala Mami also had a year like yours.
I was twenty-five, in the middle of my PhD in Chennai, when my Appa had a stroke. Everyone said, obviously you'll quit and come home. You're the daughter.
I didn't want to quit. I also couldn't just leave him. So I didn't simply refuse, and I didn't simply obey. I sat with my Amma and my brother and explained: my research was half done, and if I stopped, I would lose the scholarship. Then I listened. Amma was frightened of managing alone. My brother admitted he had been leaving it all to us women.
We made a plan. I came home every weekend on the night bus. My brother took the weekday hospital visits. I wrote my chapters beside Appa's bed on Saturdays.
It took me one year longer to finish. But I finished, and Appa was at my convocation."

qa.a: Beside Appa's bed.

qa.a: She explained her reasons, listened to her mother and brother, and made a shared plan, which let her finish her PhD while caring for her father.

Ishita had accepted the design job in Pune, her own choice, the first thing in years that was just hers. She was due to start on Monday.
Then on Wednesday her father cut his hand badly at the family printing press in Indore, and the biggest wedding-card order of the season was due in three days. The wiring kept tripping, and the only other worker was on leave.
Papa said, from the hospital bench, "So you'll stay. Forget Pune."
Ishita didn't shout, and she didn't give in. "Papa, I'll finish this order. I'll train Chotu before I go. But I'm taking the job."
She called Pranav, her new manager, and explained. He agreed she could join a week late.
She spent three nights at the press, ink on her arms, and taught her young cousin Chotu to run the cutter. Papa watched from a stool, his hand bandaged. On Friday he said, gruffly, "Your cutting is straighter than mine."

Summer update from your favourite cousin! Rosa, twenty, looked at the papers, then at their bright faces. She texted Tariq: "Can we do tomorrow? I'm so sorry."

Then Simran napped under the fan with the window open. In the evening she flew kites on the roof with her nephews, shrieking when the string cut.
